rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Dhāriyāt is a late Makkan sūrah.
rows.anchor: l-Dhāriyāt is a Makkan sūrah, most likely from the later Makkan period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is named for the scattering winds mentioned in its opening verse.
rows.anchor: The sūrah takes its name from the mention of the winds that scatter in the first verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It follows the preceding sūrah by guaranteeing Judgment, after that sūrah's conclusion on Resurrection and Gathering.
rows.anchor: vv. 5–6 guarantee the advent of the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah moves from Judgment and disbelief's fallacies to the ends of the conjecturers and reverent, creation's signs, prophetic histories, natural order, counsel, worship, and a final warning.
rows.anchor: the sūrah discusses the intellectual fallacies that lie at the heart of disbelief (vv. 7–14)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The conjecturers wander in stupefying ignorance.
rows.anchor: The conjecturers roam about in stupefying ignorance (JJ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: They are heedless of their coming fate and of what God commanded them to do.
rows.anchor: heedless of what is to befall them and of what God has commanded them to do (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusation repeats the way Pharaoh and his people tried to discredit Moses.
rows.anchor: parallels the manner in which Pharaoh and his people sought to discredit Moses in v. 39

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parallel can console Muhammad by showing that earlier messengers faced the same plight.
rows.anchor: It can be read as providing solace to the Prophet by showing him that his plight is the same as that of previous messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It can also warn Quraysh that they will share Pharaoh's followers' fate if they reject the Prophet.
rows.anchor: a warning to the Quraysh that the fate of Pharaoh and his followers will be their fate as well

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Makkans accused Muhammad of sorcery or possession, as well as other charges; other verses compare his plight to earlier prophets.
rows.anchor: the accusation that the Prophet was a sorcerer (10:2) or one possessed (52:29) is among the many accusations

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The question can mean that they urge one another to call the Prophet a sorcerer or possessed, and thus to deny him.
rows.anchor: exhort one another to saying that the Prophet is a sorcerer or one possessed (R)

rows.speaker: Most commentators
rows.claim: They read the question with wonder: would the people really urge one another to deny God and revelation?
rows.anchor: Most commentators interpret this verse as an expression of wonder that they would in fact exhort one another to denial

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: Alternatively, the question may be a negation: they do not exhort one another to it, with “it” referring to belief.
rows.anchor: it could also be understood as a negation meaning, “They do not exhort one another to it” (Āl)

rows.speaker: Most scholars
rows.claim: Most scholars consider the whole sūrah Makkan.
rows.anchor: all of al-Raḥmān to be a Makkan sūrah,

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is said to consider verse 29 Madinan.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAbbās is said to have maintained that v. 29 is from the Madinan period

rows.speaker: A minority
rows.claim: A minority considers the entire sūrah Madinan.
rows.anchor: A minority maintain that the entire sūrah is Madinan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah takes its name from al-Raḥmān, the only Divine Name directly equated with Allāh, as in 17:110.
rows.anchor: the only Divine Name to be directly equated with the Name Allāh, as in 17:110

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some regard this sūrah as an extension of al-Qamar because its opening Divine Name complements the preceding sūrah's closing name.
rows.anchor: al-Raḥmān is seen by some as an extension of al-Qamar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims call it “The Bride of the Quran” after a well-known but unauthenticated hadith.
rows.anchor: after a well-known yet unauthenticated ḥadīth that says, “For everything there is a bride

rows.speaker: Some commentaries
rows.claim: Some commentaries say the sūrah answered Makkan idolaters who asked about the Prophet's frequent invocation of the Compassionate.
rows.anchor: revealed in response to the idolaters of Makkah, who are said to have asked the meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah also recalls the idolaters' disbelief in the Compassionate, noted in 13:30.
rows.anchor: The idolaters’ disbelief in the Compassionate is also mentioned in 13:30

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–25 present God as Creator, Teacher, and Revealer and describe blessings in the created world; the sūrah then turns to heavenly blessings.
rows.anchor: The first section of the sūrah (vv. 1–25) discusses the nature of the Compassionate as Creator, Teacher, and Revealer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Duality runs through the sūrah's paired earthly and heavenly blessings, dual grammar, and refrain addressing humans and jinn.
rows.anchor: the dual form in many of the verbs and pronouns and in the refrain, addressed to both human beings and jinn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's enduring reality offsets the dualities: verses 26–27 stress that God remains while everything else passes away.
rows.anchor: vv. 26–27, which emphasize that God remains while all else fades away

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 27 is echoed by verse 78, showing that God transcends both earthly and heavenly blessings.
rows.anchor: V. 27 is then echoed in the last verse (v. 78)

rows.speaker: Most commentators
rows.claim: Most interpret the Balance as justice.
rows.anchor: The Balance is seen by most as a reference to justice (JJ, Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Other interpretations identify the Balance with religious law or the Quran.
rows.anchor: religious law ( al-sharīʿah ), or the Quran itself (Q; see 57:25c)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Balance can also signify honoring the balance and harmony of the created order.
rows.anchor: It can also be seen as a reference to honoring the balance and harmony of the created order.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The translation reads verse 8 as a subjunctive, though it may instead be imperative: “So transgress not in the balance.”
rows.anchor: v. 8 is taken as a subjunctive. But it can also be taken as an imperative

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: The subjunctive warns against tyranny and oppression; the imperative warns against withholding what is due to another.
rows.anchor: the first indicates that one must not be tyrannical and oppressive; the second indicates that one must not withhold what is due to another (Aj)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating the Balance three times underscores justice as fundamental to divine creation and human transactions.
rows.anchor: the fact that it is here thrice mentioned indicates the fundamental importance of justice

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to have said that the heavens and earth are founded on justice; no grading is given.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is reported to have said,“The heavens and the earth are founded upon justice.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥāqqah is a late Makkan sūrah, generally dated shortly after al-Mulk, and named for the Day of Judgment in its opening verses.
rows.anchor: A late Makkan sūrah, al-Ḥāqqah is generally believed to have been revealed shortly after Sūrah 67, al-Mulk.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It links to the preceding sūrah by answering the charge that the Prophet was possessed and by describing Resurrection and Judgment more fully.
rows.anchor: the later verses provide a more complete response to the charge that the Prophet was possessed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah warns through earlier deniers, describes Judgment and the differing reception of the deeds' book, then reaffirms the Quran's revealed nature.
rows.anchor: The next section (vv. 13–17) describes some aspects of the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥāqqah is an emphatic form of ḥaqq, meaning truth or reality; here it evokes the overwhelming, inevitable reality none can avoid.
rows.anchor: Undeniable Reality translates ḥāqqah, which is an emphatic form ofḥaqq, meaning “truth” or “reality.”

rows.speaker: All commentators
rows.claim: All commentators agree that the Undeniable Reality refers to Resurrection and Judgment, though they differ over the aspect meant.
rows.anchor: All commentators agree that the Undeniable Reality is a reference to the Day of Resurrection and Judgment

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: One view is that everything disbelievers rejected in earthly life will be realized and made evident.
rows.anchor: all that was rejected by disbelievers in this life will be realized and made evident (JJ)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: Another view is that everyone will see the true nature of their deeds, as in 67:11.
rows.anchor: everyone will see the true nature of their deeds, as in 67:11

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating the question, as in 101:2–3, emphasizes that the Reality exceeds mere rational comprehension.
rows.anchor: The repetition of the question in vv. 2–3, which is similar to that in 101:2–3

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The mixed fluid refers to the combination of male and female fluids.
rows.anchor: refers to the mixing of the male and female fluids (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse recalls the lowly physical origins of human beings.
rows.anchor: verses that remind human beings of the base origins of their physical nature

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The phrase about testing may instead begin a new sentence: “We will test him.”
rows.anchor: That We may test him could also be read as a new sentence: “We will test him” (JJ)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Hearing and sight are gifts and part of the test, available for obedience or disobedience.
rows.anchor: The gifts of hearing and sight are part of the test, as they may be used for obedience or disobedience (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse can indicate that the physical nature originating in mixed fluid is created to be tested.
rows.anchor: the physical nature, that which comes from a drop of mixed fluid, is created for the purpose of being tested and tried

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For how human beings are tested, the commentary directs readers to 29:2–3 and 67:2.
rows.anchor: Regarding the manner in which human beings are tested, see commentary on 29:2–3; 67:2.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse parallels 90:8–10: God provides guidance, and people are accountable for their own souls.
rows.anchor: Both passages indicate that God provides guidance for those who have eyes to see and ears to hear

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: God's guidance may come through human intellect.
rows.anchor: through the human intellect (R)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: God's guidance may come through the messengers He sends.
rows.anchor: the messengers that God sends (JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance may also come through signs in revelation, creation, and the human being.
rows.anchor: the many signs in revelation, in the created order, and within the human being

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Grateful and ungrateful may mean happy and wretched.
rows.anchor: Grateful or ungrateful indicates being either happy or wretched (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The terms may also mean believer and disbeliever, as illustrated by 18:29.
rows.anchor: or a believer or a disbeliever, as in 18:29

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah may be late Makkan, early Madinan, or a combination of both.
rows.anchor: is a late Makkan or early Madinan sūrah, or a combination of the two.

rows.speaker: Bg, IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: One account places the first four verses just after the Prophet arrived in Madinah, verses 5–28 in Madinah, and the final eight among the last verses revealed in Makkah.
rows.anchor: The first four verses were reportedly revealed just after the Prophet’s arrival in Madinah

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Another account places all verses except the first four in Makkah.
rows.anchor: all of the verses except the first four were revealed in Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name al-Muṭaffifīn means those who skim a little off the top, shortchanging others; the word derives from ṭafīf and ṭaff, the edge.
rows.anchor: deriving from ṭaff, meaning “the very edge” of something

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: More broadly, defrauders demand that their own rights be observed while neglecting others' rights, or see others' faults but not their own.
rows.anchor: those who ask that their own rights be observed, but are not willing to recognize the rights of others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah condemns shortchanging, contrasts the fates of profligates and pious people, and closes with sinners mocking the Prophet and believers.
rows.anchor: Beginning with a condemnation of those who shortchange others (vv. 1–6)

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: When the Prophet first reached Madinah, its people were notorious defrauders; after revelation of these verses, they weighed honestly.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAbbās said, “When the Prophet first moved to Madinah, its inhabitants were the worst kind of defrauders

rows.speaker: Abū Hurayrah
rows.claim: The verses refer directly to a man who used separate scales for buying and selling.
rows.anchor: According to Abū Hurayrah, these verses refer directly to a man who had two scales

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet linked covenant-breaking with enemies, judging apart from revelation with poverty, fornication with death, fraud with crop failure and famine, and withholding alms with withheld rain; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: The Prophet recited them to the citizens of Madinah and said, “Five for five.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning extends beyond commerce: anyone who intentionally falls short in anything ordained by God may face shame and suffering.
rows.anchor: shame and suffering will befall anyone who intentionally falls short in any matter according to what has been ordained by God

rows.speaker: Ibn Masʿūd
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd compares prayer to a measure: completing it brings full reward, while reducing it recalls the warning against defrauders.
rows.anchor: Ibn Masʿūd, a Companion of the Prophet and early Quranic commentator, said, “Prayer is a measure.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A noncanonical reading treats both instances of “them” as subjects rather than direct objects: “when they measure or weigh, they stint.”
rows.anchor: can be read as an affirmation of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse may be read with “but” to distinguish believers' fate from that of disbelievers.
rows.anchor: Some say this verse should read, “but those who believe . . .” to distinguish the fate of believers from that of disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “save those who” distinguishes disbelievers who repent from those who do not.
rows.anchor: Others say that it should be “save those who . . .” to distinguish the disbelievers who repent from those who do not

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For “reward unceasing,” the commentary refers readers to 41:8 and 95:6.
rows.anchor: For the meaning of reward unceasing, see 41:8c; 95:6c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This statement answers the oaths in the first five verses.
rows.anchor: This verse constitutes the response to the oaths in the first five verses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kanūd means either barren land where nothing grows or a petty, miserly person.
rows.anchor: Kanūd, here translated ungrateful, indicates a land where nothing grows or a person who is petty and miserly.

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: “Truth” can mean God.
rows.anchor: truth can mean God (Q)

rows.speaker: Bg, Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: “Truth” can mean the Quran.
rows.anchor: the Quran (Bg, Q, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Bg, Ṭs
rows.claim: “Truth” can mean faith and professing Divine Unity.
rows.anchor: faith and professing Divine Unity (Bg, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: It may mean telling those one leaves at death, “die not except in submission,” as in 3:102.
rows.anchor: at the moment of death one says to those one leaves behind, and die not except in submission (3:102; Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers are elsewhere commanded to be patient and vie in patience, as in 3:200.
rows.anchor: Elsewhere believers are commanded, Be patient, vie in patience (3:200).

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Exhorting one another to patience can mean sustaining religious practice through hardship and opposition.
rows.anchor: encouraging one another in maintaining religious practice in the face of difficulties and opposition (R)

rows.speaker: Sh
rows.claim: The paired exhortations parallel belief in God and righteous deeds, and extend to what must be known and done.
rows.anchor: The exhortation to truth and patience can thus be seen as an exhortation paralleling that between belief in God and performing righteous deeds (Sh)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Righteous deeds arise from and remain joined to faith in God; the sūrah emphasizes truth and patience amid widespread spiritual darkness and personal crises.
rows.anchor: righteous deeds are believed to arise from and are always conjoined with faith and belief in God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Humazah is an early Makkan sūrah, probably revealed after al-Qiyāmah, and named for its opening condemnation of slanderers.
rows.anchor: an early Makkan sūrah, most likely revealed after Sūrah 75, al-Qiyāmah

rows.speaker: Q, Z
rows.claim: One reported occasion is al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, who slandered people both to their faces and behind their backs.
rows.anchor:
It was reportedly revealed regarding a man by the name of al-
Akhnas ibn Shurayq (Q, Z)

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: Another reported occasion is al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, a Quraysh leader hostile to the Prophet who slandered him openly and in his absence.
rows.anchor: revealed in relation to al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Some regard it as a general condemnation unrelated to one particular person or event.
rows.anchor: Others say that it is a general condemnation, not one revealed in relation to any specific person or instance (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Even if revelation concerned a specific event, its application may remain general.
rows.anchor: it is permissible to view something revealed in relation to a specific instance as having a general application (Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah focuses on the torment awaiting people who spend worldly life hoarding wealth.
rows.anchor: focus upon the torment that awaits one who spends the life of this world hoarding wealth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hoarder's punishment is vividly described in 9:34–35: hoarded gold and silver brand their owners in Hell.
rows.anchor: The punishment for those who hoard is most vividly described in 9:34–35

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī explains the contented life as a life in Paradise that the person is pleased with.
rows.anchor: يقول : في عيشة قد رضيها في الجنة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda glosses the contented life as being in Paradise; the source gives no grading.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة { فَهُوَ فِي عِيشَةٍ رَاضِيَةٍ } يعني : في الجنة
